Use LLMs to turn unstructured user data into structured preference representations, then store and use them in a knowledge graph for recommendation. One path is to extract user-preference triples from conversations, ideally RDF-compliant and linked to identifiers such as Wikidata, to build a personal knowledge graph; the resulting graph can then be evaluated directly in downstream recommendation tasks [2]. Another is to have LLMs generate semantic profiles or compressed rationales from diverse knowledge sources, attach those profiles to entities in a knowledge graph, and use graph aggregation plus profile-preference matching to improve recommendations [1].

The papers differ in what they graph and how they use it. Some focus on explicit PKG construction from conversational data for privacy-preserving user modeling [2], while others enrich entity- and user-side representations inside broader recommender KGs and propagate preferences through the graph [1, 3]. Related work also suggests adding graph-based community summaries for persona prompts [5] or emphasizing inspectable, revisable, portable user representations for governable personalization [8].
